methodological_rigor.justification: The study uses an appropriate design for prognostic modeling (retrospective cohort with LASSO Cox regression and multivariable Cox model), with reasonable preprocessing (1037 features reduced to five via LASSO), reporting of C-index with 95% CIs, calibration curves, DCA, and subgroup analyses. However, the design is single-center retrospective with only internal 7:3 split validation (testing n=39) and no external cohort; no a priori sample size or power calculation is reported, and only 23.1% of 130 patients experienced the endpoint, yielding roughly 21 events in training against five radiomic features plus clinical covariates—risking overfitting given typical EPV guidelines. Multiplicity across 1037 features is handled only via LASSO without explicit permutation testing or optimism correction (e.g., bootstrap), and the testing-cohort time-ROC CIs exceed 1.0 (e.g., 3-yr AUC 0.954, 95% CI 0.879–1.029), indicating unstable estimates. Dichotomization of continuous variables (RPE, risk score) via X-tile on the same training data without correction for optimism further weakens the statistical treatment.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective prognostic cohort study with internal validation only, which corresponds to Oxford LoE 2b (low-quality / internally validated prognostic cohort). The clinical question—predicting life-threatening cerebral herniation in nasopharyngeal carcinoma survivors with radiation-induced cystic necrosis—is genuinely important for a narrow but high-morbidity population, and the model could plausibly inform surveillance intensity and surgical timing as the authors suggest. However, the endpoint (herniation on imaging) is a hard but surrogate-adjacent outcome without reported downstream OS/QoL impact, and no prospective validation or decision-impact study exists; recommendations about 3- vs 6-month imaging intervals and early surgery are therefore hypothesis-generating.

reporting_quality.justification: TRIPOD is the applicable standard because the study develops and internally validates a multivariable prognostic prediction model. Many key TRIPOD items are addressed: study design, participant eligibility (via supplement), predictors, outcome definition, statistical methods, model specification (explicit risk score formula), calibration curves, DCA, and discussion of limitations. Notable gaps include absence of protocol/registration, no sample size justification, limited reporting of missing data handling, no formal optimism correction/bootstrap, and the cutoff-derivation strategy is not fully transparent. No data or code availability statement is retained in the blinded text and no public repository is referenced, so reproducibility posture is weak.

novelty_literature.justification: The empirical novelty is the specific endpoint—cerebral herniation—within the RCN population, which the authors reasonably argue has not been directly targeted before. However, the field already contains closely related radiomics work in RCN and radiation-induced brain injury from NPC: ref 18 (radiomics for bevacizumab response in brain necrosis), ref 19 (MRI radiomics predicting cystic brain radionecrosis in NPC), and ref 25 (radiomics for methylprednisolone response). Methodologically the pipeline (T2WI, LASSO-Cox, nomogram, calibration, DCA) is standard, so novelty is a meaningful but incremental extension of prior radiomic work to a new, clinically significant endpoint rather than a conceptual or methodological leap.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written with a logical IMRaD structure; the abstract is quantitatively grounded (C-index 0.841/0.867, cohort sizes, follow-up duration) and accurately summarizes the main findings. Acronyms are expanded on first use (RCN, RPE, LASSO), methods are coherent though reliant on supplements, and the discussion appropriately contextualizes corticosteroid findings and VEGF-mediated enhancement mechanisms. Minor issues include some repetition between results and discussion, occasional awkward phrasing in the abstract's opening summary paragraph, and figure captions are referenced but their standalone utility cannot be fully assessed. Overall it reads as a well-organized, publication-ready prognostic-radiomics manuscript.

key_strengths: Addresses a clinically important and underexplored endpoint (cerebral herniation in RCN) in NPC survivors
Methodologically standard radiomics pipeline with LASSO-Cox, calibration, DCA, and explicit nomogram/risk-score formula
Good discriminative performance (C-index 0.841 training, 0.867 testing) with subgroup consistency
Clear, well-organized writing with quantitatively grounded abstract and transparent limitations section
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with internal 7:3 split only; testing cohort of 39 (likely ~9 events) yields unstable estimates (AUC CIs > 1.0)
No a priori sample size/power calculation and no formal optimism correction (bootstrap) for the model
Multiple data-driven dichotomizations (RPE 28.5%, risk score cutoffs) via X-tile on training data without correction, risking optimistic cutoffs
No external validation; generalizability to other centers/tumors unaddressed empirically
No data or code availability statement; reproducibility posture is weak
Novelty is incremental—radiomic prediction in RCN/RIBI has been reported for other endpoints
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competently executed, well-written single-center prognostic radiomics study with a clinically meaningful but narrow niche; discrimination is solid but internal-only validation, small test set, and standard methodology place it best within Tier 3 (specialty oncology/imaging journals) with minor revisions to strengthen reporting and reproducibility.
